# Draft:French Archaeological Mission in the United Arab Emirate

The French Archaeological Mission in the United Arab Emirates is a French state-funded archaeological research programme operating in the United Arab Emirates since 1976, placed under the authority of the French Ministry of Europe and Foreign Affairs. Over nearly five decades, a succession of French missions has conducted excavations and surveys across five emirates—Abu Dhabi, Sharjah, Umm al-Quwain, Ras al-Khaimah, and Fujairah—covering periods from the Neolithic to the Islamic era.
Background
The earliest modern archaeological work in the UAE predates French involvement and took place before the country's unification in December 1971. The first documented excavations were conducted from 1958–1959 by a Danish team led by Professors P. V. Glob and G. Bibby, invited by Sheikh Shakhbut bin Sultan Al Nahyan, then ruler of Abu Dhabi. Working on Umm an-Nar Island (Sas Al Nakhl), they uncovered a Bronze Age funerary complex that gave its name to the Umm al-Nar culture (c. 2600–2000 BCE). The Danish mission continued until 1965, was briefly resumed by an Iraqi mission in 1975, and subsequently taken over by the Department of Antiquities of Al Ain in 1979 and by the Department of Culture and Tourism (DCT) Abu Dhabi from 2020. Between 1961 and 1971, Danish archaeologists also explored the Al Ain region around Jebel Hafeet, identifying the older Hafit culture (c. 3300–2600 BCE). The oases of Al Ain have been inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 2011.
History
Foundation and the Abu Dhabi mission (1976–1985)
The French Archaeological Mission in Abu Dhabi was established in 1976 on the initiative of Professor J. Deshayes of the Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne. Under the direction of Professor Serge Cleuziou, working in cooperation with the Abu Dhabi authorities, the mission focused primarily on the Al Ain region, one of the archaeologically richest areas of the Arabian Peninsula. Until 1985, Cleuziou's team excavated habitation sites and collective burials of the Hafit and Umm an-Nar cultures at the Hili oasis. In parallel, an important Iron Age site (c. 1300–300 BCE) was investigated at Rumeilah by R. Boucharlat and M. Mouton.
Expansion to other emirates (1986–1994)
French archaeological initiatives extended to additional emirates during the 1980s, covering sites from the Neolithic to the Islamic period:
* The French Archaeological Mission in Sharjah (1986–1995), directed by R. Boucharlat and subsequently M. Mouton, focused on Mleiha, a major centre of the Late Pre-Islamic period (350 BCE – 350 CE), and the Iron Age site of Rumeilah.
* The French Archaeological Mission at ed-Dur (1993–1994), directed by O. Lecomte, investigated ed-Dur in Umm al-Quwain, another major Pre-Islamic centre.
* The French Archaeological Mission at Julfar (1988–1995), directed by C. Hardy-Guilbert, excavated and studied Julfar, a major Islamic-period port city of the 14th–15th centuries in Ras al-Khaimah.
Consolidation (1995–2018)
In 1995, S. Méry — formerly a member of Cleuziou's team — reactivated the Mission archéologique française à Abu Dhabi. Excavations resumed at the collective Bronze Age tombs of the Hili oasis until 2006. Simultaneously, from 1999, A. Benoist initiated a research programme on Iron Age populations in the mountainous areas of Fujairah and Ras al-Khaimah. The two operations were merged into the French Archaeological Mission in the United Arab Emirates, coordinated by S. Méry until 2018.
Following the definitive end of the Abu Dhabi operations in 2006, the mission's research strategies shifted towards the Arabian Neolithic period (c. 6500–3300 BCE). This built on earlier excavations initiated in 1990–1992 by R. Boucharlat's mission and resumed from 2002 by V. Charpentier (INRAP) at the site of Akab (Jazirat al-Ghallah) in the coastal region of Umm al-Quwain emirate. Excavations at this site revealed a major sanctuary dating to the end of the Neolithic (c. 3500 BCE), constructed entirely from the bones of dugongs, representing the oldest known ritual sanctuary in Arabia. This structure marks the end of occupation of a fishermen's settlement whose foundations date back at least a millennium earlier. Between 2009 and 2018, older Neolithic habitation sites (from c. 5400/5200 BCE) in the form of large shell middens were discovered and excavated along the coastal dune belt extending from Umm al-Quwain to Ras al-Khaimah.
The Iron Age fieldwork in the northern emirates continued between 2000 and 2020 under the successive direction of A. Benoist (2000–2015) and J. Charbonnier (2016–2020). Two major Iron Age centres were investigated in the localities of Bithnah and Masafi, comprising fortified habitations, oasis exploitation zones, irrigation systems, and sanctuaries.
Reactivation (Since 2024)
The French Archaeological Mission in the United Arab Emirates was reactivated in 2024 by Kevin Lidour, then in post at DCT Abu Dhabi, who leads a new excavation programme at the Neolithic site of Jazirat al-Ghallah.

Principal sites
Arabian Neolithic (c. 6500–3300 BCE)
* Jazirat al-Ghallah (Akab), Umm al-Quwain: Shell midden settlement of fishermen dated c. 4600–3500/3300 BCE, notable for one of the largest ichthyofaunal assemblages from the Arabian Neolithic (over 37,000 fish remains, 50+ species), early pearling evidence, and a dugong bone mound interpreted as the oldest known ritual sanctuary in Arabia (c. 3500-3300 BCE).
* Umm al-Quwain UAQ2, Umm al-Quwain: Stratified Neolithic shell midden and graveyard occupied c. 5500–3800 BCE, one of the longest Neolithic sequences known in the Arabian Gulf, with the oldest securely dated archaeological pearl (c. 5500 BCE) and one of the oldest known graveyards in the region.
Bronze Age (c. 3300–1300 BCE)
* Hili, Al Ain (Abu Dhabi): Umm an-Nar collective tombs. Hili N, a pit-grave containing approximately 700 individuals with imports from the Indus Valley and Mesopotamia, was one of the mission's most significant excavations.
Iron Age (c. 1300–300 BCE)
* Bithnah, Fujairah: Fortified Iron Age settlement with associated oasis exploitation and irrigation systems.
* Masafi, Fujairah: Multi-period site documenting Late Bronze Age and Early Iron Age coastal-hinterland exchange networks.
* Rumeilah, Al Ain: Major Iron Age settlement investigated in parallel with the Hili Bronze Age programme.
Late Pre-Islamic period (350 BCE – 350 CE)
* Mleiha, Sharjah: One of the largest and most significant Late Pre-Islamic sites in the UAE, excavated 1986–1995.
* Ed-Dur, Umm al-Quwain: Major coastal Pre-Islamic settlement investigated 1993–1994.
Islamic period
* Julfar, Ras al-Khaimah: Important port city and trading entrepôt of the 14th–15th centuries CE, one of the most extensively excavated Islamic-period sites in the Gulf.
